drafts.neutral_framing: Should Melbourne Beach pair its stormwater repairs with living filters — oyster reefs, living shorelines, or nutrient-removing media — where its pipes empty into the lagoon?
drafts.final_wording: Every storm drain in town empties toward the Indian River Lagoon. Should the town pilot a living filter — an oyster reef, a living shoreline, or a nitrogen-removing filter bed — at one stormwater outfall, with water tests before and after?
drafts.final_wording_note: Framed around a pilot the town can choose however its drainage work is paid for. It does not ask about the November 3 bond, which is an active ballot measure.
shaping_notes: A question about a method, not about any person, candidate, or ballot measure. The bond referendum is deliberately left out; this question stands whether the bond passes or not.
Grounded in local records: the town’s own description of failing pipes that send rain into the lagoon, Brevard Zoo’s oyster reef at Ryckman Park, and the county’s BAM filter results.
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion — verification tiers arrive with the full voting layer.
drafts.background: The town says many of its storm pipes are decades old, undersized, corroding or sealed off, sending rainwater “into the Indian River Lagoon.” Nitrogen and phosphorus in that water feed the algae blooms that killed the lagoon’s seagrass — and, from 2020 to 2022, starved 1,255 manatees. A 900-square-foot oyster reef at Ryckman Park drew about 40,000 oysters in a year. See Our water.

founding_solutions.title: Pilot one living filter at a Basin 1 outfall
founding_solutions.summary: Pick one outfall from the town’s Basin 1 stormwater work and add a filter — biosorption activated media (BAM), an oyster reef, or a living shoreline — with nitrogen and phosphorus tests before and after, and apply to the county’s lagoon program for cost-share.

drafts.neutral_framing: Should the Brevard County jail’s farm and kitchen work count toward a college certificate people can finish after release?
drafts.final_wording: The Sheriff’s Farm already grows food for the Brevard County jail, and the jail already offers trade certificates. Should the Sheriff and Eastern Florida State College pilot a short farm-and-kitchen certificate that people can start inside and finish after release?
drafts.final_wording_note: Framed around two programs that already exist. Taking part would be offered, never required.
shaping_notes: A question about a program design — not about any person, candidate, or ballot measure.
Grounded in the Sheriff’s own program list and budget. Melbourne Beach has no jail; people arrested in town go to the county jail, which town residents help pay for through county taxes.
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion — verification tiers arrive with the full voting layer.
drafts.background: The Brevard County jail holds over 1,600 people a day; in February 2023, 86.8% had not been convicted. The Sheriff asked for $61.5 million to run it in FY2025-26. It already offers GED classes, ServSafe and OSHA certificates, barbering, and the Sheriff’s Farm. See Jails & prisons.

founding_solutions.title: A farm-and-kitchen certificate with Eastern Florida State College
founding_solutions.summary: Pair the Sheriff’s Farm and the jail kitchen with a short college certificate in horticulture or food safety, offered to anyone eligible who wants it, and track who finishes, who gets hired, and who comes back.

drafts.neutral_framing: Should Melbourne Beach post its payments — who was paid, how much, and for what — as data anyone can download?
drafts.final_wording: Melbourne Beach posts its budgets and audits, but no list of payments was found online. Should the town post its check register every month as a spreadsheet anyone can download?
drafts.final_wording_note: Framed around a step the town can take on its own: publishing records it already keeps.
shaping_notes: A question about the town’s own disclosure format — not about any person, candidate, or ballot measure.
Grounded in what was and was not found: budgets FY2022–FY2027 and audits 2023–2025 are on the town’s Finance page; no check register was found (Docket #13).
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion — verification tiers arrive with the full voting layer.
drafts.background: The town’s budget shows how much each department is given — $5.36 million across its funds this year. It doesn’t show what was bought or from whom. Not found online means not found yet, not hidden (Docket #13).

founding_solutions.title: Post the check register monthly
founding_solutions.summary: Each month, post the town’s payments — vendor, amount, date, and what was bought — as a downloadable spreadsheet next to the budgets on the Finance page.
